newsitem.title: FRANCE: Le Pen says leftist win in France will help Front.
newsitem.headline: Le Pen says leftist win in France will help Front.

text.p: Far-right leader Jean-Marie Le Pen said on Thursday that a leftist win in France's National Assembly election would help his National Front party by paralysing the country and blocking its drift toward European integration.

A period of cohabitation, forcing conservative President Jacques Chirac to work with a leftist government, "would tie Chirac's hands on Europe, and will lead to a new dissolution within a year," Le Pen said on Radio Luxembourg.
"And perhaps the next time around, the National Front will be better placed to win power than it is now," he said.
Le Pen has urged his supporters to vote for leftist candidates in the second round of France's May 25-June 1 snap election, saying his top priority is to deprive Chirac of a majority in parliament.
But polls find that Front voters, who make up about 13 percent to 15 percent of the total, are behaving as if they want the centre-right to remain in power.
Pollsters say the Front will win at most three seats in the 577-seat National Assembly, where it now has none.

But they add that its supporters are in a position to play a decisive role in the election by deciding close votes in the second-round vote in constituencies where Front candidates have not survived the first-round vote.

Several recent polls have found that large -- and growing -- numbers of National Front voters are shifting to the centre-right candidate in the second round rather than to the leftist candidate, as Le Pen has urged.
Le Pen on Thursday played down the advice he has given supporters.
"In the second round they will do what they want. I will offer my opinion, and they will follow it or not, as they wish," he said.

"I have merely said that it would be preferable for the French people if this were a cohabitation government with a leftist majority, as this would stop our deadly drift towards the globalisation of Maastricht."
Le Pen opposes European integration and particularly a single European currency, predicting it will result in a loss of national identity and put France's destiny in the hands of outsiders.

"If France became a state like Alabama or Texas, and the president a governor, perhaps he (Chirac) could get used to this but not the French people, because they would no longer be able to determine their destiny," he said. "They would be dependent on others."
